extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and students of 19th-century popular astronomy/science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evidential standards used to assess the plausibility of the Nebular Hypothesis for the origin of the Solar System, as presented in a 19th‑century popular-science exposition. Focuses on observational concordance, mechanical plausibility, probabilistic arguments, and experimental analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movements of the planets in same direction and plane
rubrics_metrics.description: “The movements of the planets in the same direction and in orbits approaching to the same plane.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace enumerates this as a leading evidence for a common genetic process; the immense uniformity of planetary motions is taken as highly improbable under chance or arbitrary arrangement and supports an evolutionary/genetic origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movements of the satellites in same direction as the planets
rubrics_metrics.description: “The movements of the satellites in the same direction as those of the planets.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful hypothesis should explain why satellites circulate in the same sense as their primaries and why their orbital planes approximate the primaries' equators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of rotations with orbital motions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The movements of rotation of these various bodies and of the sun in the same direction as the orbital motions, and mostly in planes little different.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis must account for the general concordance between axial rotation directions and orbital directions (including the Sun), not merely orbital arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small eccentricities of planetary and satellite orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: “The small eccentricities of the orbits of the planets and satellites, as contrasted with the great eccentricities of the cometary orbits.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A viable origin theory should explain why planetary and satellite orbits are nearly circular while cometary orbits are highly eccentric; this contrast is diagnostic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concordance with cometary orbital characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational argument that many cometary orbits classed as parabolic may in fact be extremely eccentric ellipses, implying comets could be products of the same genesis (detached nebulous fragments) rather than visitors from infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis should account for comet origin and orbital distribution; recognizes observational limits (near-perihelion observations may misclassify ellipses as parabolas) and predicts many comet orbits are elliptical if comets arise from the nebula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical plausibility via rotating spheroid and ring-detachment model
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace's model: a vast rotating spheroid of rarefied matter contracting increases rotation, produces centrifugal equatorial rings which detach and later aggregate into planets and satellites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory must be mechanically coherent: contraction → increased rotation → ring formation → ring rupture/aggregation into bodies. The chain of mechanical steps and their consequences (rings→planets→satellites→Sun) are essential explanatory elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental analogy: Plateau's rotating-fluid ring experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dr. Plateau has shown that when a mass of fluid is ... made to rotate with adequate velocity, it will form detached rings; and that these rings will break up into spheroids which turn on their axes in the same direction with the central mass.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laboratory demonstrations that rotating fluids form rings which disintegrate into spheroids are cited as experimental support for the mechanical sequence asserted by the hypothesis; presence of such analogues strengthens plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for progressive decrease of orbital inclinations inward
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that flocculi from an irregular nebula would start in innumerable planes and that gradual vortical motion produces a gradual establishment of a common plane, with outer portions retaining more independent inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis should predict that inclinations decrease on average toward the Sun (earlier detached rings differ more from the average plane), matching observed inclination trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for anomalies in axial rotations (Uranus/Neptune) via ring shape/velocity differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation that differences in ring sectional form (hoop-shaped vs quoit-shaped) and relative angular velocities of inner and outer ring parts can yield prograde, retrograde, or highly inclined rotation axes; thus apparent anomalies are explicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A credible theory must allow for exceptions and provide mechanisms (e.g., ring geometry, differences in absolute/angular velocities) that can produce axial tilts or retrograde rotation in specific cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of rotation speed with planet mass and ring properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that, contrary to naive expectation, the Nebular Hypothesis predicts large planets rotate rapidly while small ones rotate slowly, because wide genetic rings and long travel distances impart higher axial velocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis should predict observed rotational periods (e.g., Jupiter <10 h, Saturn ~10.5 h, terrestrial planets longer) based on ring breadth, oblateness, and amount of material aggregated from distant regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satellites repeat planetary relations and size ordering (miniature systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that each set of satellites repeats in miniature the relations of the planets to the Sun, both in directional/planar relations and in ordering of sizes (outer satellites larger, inner smaller).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory must explain the parallelism between primary and secondary systems (size ordering, orbital arrangement), which undermines teleological/design explanations and supports a common physical genesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict satellite abundance from centrifugal/centripetal ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Detachment of rings (and thus satellite-forming tendency) depends on the ratio of centrifugal force to gravitation at the equator during concentration; where this ratio is greatest more rings/satellites will form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative calculation of centrifugal/centripetal ratios should approximately indicate which planets will have many satellites (Saturn, Jupiter) and which few or none (Mercury); observed counts are compared to these predictions (with discussion of anomalies like Venus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain synchronous rotations and orbital resonances of satellites
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace's arguments that phenomena such as the Moon's synchronous rotation and the arithmetic relation among Jupiter's satellites' mean motions (if mean angular velocity of first + twice that of third = three times that of second) are unlikely by chance and should be explained by the genesis process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory hypothesis should yield mechanisms (dynamical evolution, tidal interaction, resonant capture) to account for locked rotations and specific resonant relations among satellites rather than treating them as accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturn's rings as extant witnesses with expected dynamical relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Saturn's rings are permanent forms of aggregation analogous to stages planets once passed; their movements and the ratio of Saturn's rotation to ring revolution (427 to 438) accord with expectations from the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory gains strength if observed ring characteristics (location, dynamics, rotation period relations) are exactly the sort it predicts; rings serve as direct observational evidence of the proposed processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for observational/parameter uncertainty in anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that discrepancies (e.g., Venus lacking an observed satellite, earlier wrong density estimate for Mars) may arise from observational elusion or errors in input parameters, and that only general congruity is to be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust hypothesis must tolerate some mismatches due to measurement uncertainty, incomplete observations, or variable formation conditions; resolving anomalies may require revised input data or improved observations rather than discarding the overall theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for comet composition and permanence vs dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that small detached fragments of nebulous matter (with small mutual gravitation) will remain in their original diffused state (as appears to be the case for non-periodic comets), while larger aggregations can evolve into denser bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis should explain compositional and behavioral differences among comet classes (periodic vs non-periodic) in terms of mass, mutual gravitation, evolving heat dissipation, and origin (e.g., swarms of meteors enveloped in aeriform matter).
